title: Backend Development
blurb: The server side — APIs, databases, auth, and how the web really works.

lessons.title: HTTP fundamentals
lessons.explain: HTTP is request/response. Methods signal intent: GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes.
objectives: Use the correct HTTP method and interpret status codes for a request
Explain how HTTP methods changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect HTTP methods with status codes and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Using GET for an operation that changes server state -- GET requests can be cached, prefetched, or retried automatically.

lessons.explain: REST models your app as resources (nouns) accessed via URLs and HTTP verbs. JSON is the standard data format — key/value pairs, arrays, nested objects.

lessons.title: Building an API with FastAPI
lessons.explain: FastAPI turns Python functions into HTTP endpoints with automatic validation and docs. A path operation maps a URL+method to a function.
objectives: Define a path operation with FastAPI that validates input automatically
Explain how FastAPI changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect FastAPI with path operations and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Skipping type hints on path operation parameters -- FastAPI's automatic validation and docs generation depend on them.

lessons.title: Servers: what happens when a request arrives
objectives: Trace a request from the network to your application code
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: middleware, environment-based configuration, structured logging.
Explain how server process changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect server process with port and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A server is a process listening on a port for incoming connections. When a request arrives, the OS hands it to your server process, which parses the HTTP request, routes it to the right handler function based on method+path, runs your code, and sends a response back down the same connection.
examples:
# conceptually, before any framework:
# 1. socket accepts a connection
# 2. read raw bytes, parse method+path+headers
# 3. match against your routes
# 4. call the matching function, get a response
# 5. write the response bytes back, close/keep-alive the connection
commonMistakes: Assuming 'the server' is one mysterious black box — it's normal application code, listening on a port, that you could largely write yourself.
lessons.careerRelevance: This mental model is exactly what interviewers probe when they ask 'what happens when you type a URL and hit enter.' These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Databases & persistence for backend services
objectives: Explain why backend services need persistent storage
Connect a basic ORM/query layer conceptually
Explain how persistence changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect persistence with ORM and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Persistence means keeping application state beyond the lifetime of one process. In a backend service, an ORM can map application objects to database rows, but the database schema is still a production contract that changes over time.
examples:
# raw SQL
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", (user_id,))

# ORM equivalent (conceptually)
user = User.objects.get(id=user_id)
commonMistakes: Storing real user data only in memory 'to move fast' — a restart, deploy, or crash means total data loss.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every real backend service needs this; it's the difference between a toy demo and a production service.

lessons.title: Authentication: sessions vs tokens
objectives: Contrast session-based and token-based (JWT) authentication
Explain how session changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect session with JWT and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Authentication proves who's making a request. Session-based auth stores a session ID in a cookie, which the server looks up against server-side state on every request.
commonMistakes: Storing sensitive data unencrypted inside a JWT payload — JWTs are signed (tamper-proof) but NOT encrypted by default; anyone can decode and read the payload.
lessons.careerRelevance: Choosing and correctly implementing auth is one of the most consequential decisions in any backend service.
lessons.explain: Authentication proves who's making a request. Session-based auth stores a session ID in a cookie, which the server looks up against server-side state on every request.

lessons.title: Security & input validation
objectives: Identify and prevent the most common backend vulnerabilities
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: CORS, password hashing, safe file upload/download.
Explain how SQL injection changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SQL injection with input validation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Never trust client input. SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated directly into a query instead of using parameterized queries.
examples:
# VULNERABLE:
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{user_input}'"

# SAFE: parameterized query, the driver handles escaping
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", (user_input,))
commonMistakes: Building your own string-concatenation 'escaping' instead of using parameterized queries/prepared statements — this is how real SQL injection breaches happen, repeatedly, in production.
lessons.careerRelevance: Security questions are now a standard part of backend interview loops, not a specialist-only topic. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Scaling & backend architecture
objectives: Identify the first few scaling levers for a growing backend service
Explain how caching changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect caching with load balancing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Backend scaling is not only adding more servers. Caches reduce repeated work, load balancers distribute requests, read replicas can move read traffic away from the primary database, and background-job queues move slow work out of the request path.
examples:
# request path once it starts scaling:
users -> load balancer -> [server, server, server] -> cache -> database (+ read replicas)
#                                                    -> background queue (emails, etc.)
commonMistakes: Prematurely over-engineering for scale you don't have yet — profile and scale the ACTUAL bottleneck, not a guessed one.
lessons.careerRelevance: Scaling questions are a staple of system-design interviews, even for internship-level SWE roles.

lessons.title: Async FastAPI, concurrency & request safety
objectives: Use async endpoints appropriately and identify when shared mutable state needs synchronization
Explain how async def changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect async def with await and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Async web frameworks let one process keep serving other requests while a request waits on non-blocking I/O. Use async def when the libraries you call are async and you have many I/O waits; CPU-heavy work should not block the event loop.
lessons.example:
from fastapi import FastAPI
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/health")
async def health():
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return {"ok": True}
commonMistakes: Adding async to a function that still calls long blocking libraries.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

description: The server side — APIs, databases, auth, and how the web really works.

interviewPreparation.q: Walk me through what happens between a client sending a request and your server sending a response.
interviewPreparation.a: DNS resolves the domain, a TCP (or QUIC) connection is established, the server's web layer routes the request to the right handler, the handler validates input, does whatever business logic/DB work is needed, and constructs a response with the right status code and body, which travels back over the same connection.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide between session-based and token-based authentication for a new API?
interviewPreparation.a: Sessions are simpler and easy to revoke server-side, but require server-side state, which complicates horizontal scaling. Tokens (like JWTs) are stateless and scale more easily across multiple servers, but revocation before expiry is harder. For a single web app, sessions are often simpler; for a mobile app plus web app plus third-party integrations, tokens usually win.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you prevent SQL injection in practice, not just in theory?
interviewPreparation.a: Use parameterized queries or an ORM that parameterizes for you by default -- never build SQL by concatenating user input into a string. Input validation is a second layer of defense, but parameterization is the actual fix, since validation alone is easy to miss an edge case on.

interviewPreparation.q: A service that was fine at low traffic is now timing out under load. How do you start diagnosing it?
interviewPreparation.a: Check whether it's the app layer or the database first -- slow query logs and connection pool exhaustion are common root causes that look like 'the app is slow' from the outside. Only after ruling out the database would I look at app-level concurrency or a genuinely undersized server.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the N+1 query problem, and how do you fix it?
interviewPreparation.a: It's when fetching a list of N items triggers one query for the list plus N additional queries, one per item, instead of a single batched query -- often invisible until traffic or data volume grows. Fixed with a join, a single IN-clause query, or an ORM's eager-loading feature instead of querying inside a loop.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you approach testing a backend service beyond manually hitting endpoints with a tool like Postman?
interviewPreparation.a: Automated tests for the core business logic and endpoints, including edge cases (invalid input, unauthorized access, empty results) -- not just the happy path. Manual testing is fine for exploration, but it doesn't scale and doesn't catch regressions when you change something later.

capstone.title: Design, secure, test, and deploy a production-style backend service
capstone.description: Take a real backend service idea (not a toy CRUD demo) and carry it further than a typical project: a documented API architecture, real authentication, automated tests (not just manual poking), input validation against common attacks, and an actual deployment -- plus monitoring notes on what you'd watch in production. This should read like something you'd walk an interviewer through, not just a repo that runs.
deliverables: A short architecture doc: endpoints, data model, and at least one explicit scaling/reliability trade-off you made
Authentication implemented correctly (hashed passwords, proper token handling -- not a toy check)
An automated test suite covering at least the core endpoints, not just happy-path manual testing
Input validation demonstrably closing at least one real vulnerability class (e.g. SQL injection, as covered in this course)
A real deployment (even a free-tier one) plus a short note on what you'd monitor if this were in production
capstone.portfolioTips: This is the project to walk through in a backend interview end-to-end -- requirements, trade-offs, what broke, how you'd scale it further. A working deployed link plus this narrative is far stronger than a longer list of smaller, undocumented projects.

industryUsage.usage: Runs backend services at massive scale across its product portfolio, where the reliability and scaling fundamentals covered in this course (not just getting an API working) are the actual bar for backend engineering roles.
Built its reputation on backend API reliability and careful authentication/authorization design, since a payments API failing or leaking data has direct, serious consequences.
As a fintech, treats backend input validation and authentication as first-class concerns rather than an afterthought, given the regulatory and security stakes of financial data.
